text: You've now learned about shared, exclusive, update, intent, and schema locks, plus granularity and escalation — all described in the abstract or glimpsed briefly. This lesson makes all of it concrete with one real view: sys.dm_tran_locks.
This is a dynamic management view showing SQL Server's actual lock state at the exact moment you query it — every lock currently granted or waiting, system-wide.

Four columns matter most. resource_type tells you what's locked — a whole object, a page, a key for an indexed row. request_mode tells you which lock type — S, X, U, the intent locks, the schema locks, matching exactly what this chapter has covered. request_status is GRANT if the lock is actually held, or WAIT if the session is blocked. And request_session_id is the SPID, letting you trace a row back to a real session.

Revisit the exclusive-lock scenario from a few lessons back. Session A holds an open UPDATE transaction; Session B's SELECT against the same row blocks. Query sys.dm_tran_locks from a third window, filtered to both session IDs, and you'll see it directly: Session A's row shows KEY, X, GRANT. Session B's row shows KEY, S, WAIT.

That's exactly why this view matters on the job. When something is just hanging in production, this is the first place to check — not to guess, but to actually confirm it's a locking issue and identify precisely which session holds the lock everyone else is waiting on.
Next up: what happens when two sessions are each the one the other is waiting on, with no way out — the deadlock.
